11679-the-white-road-to-verdun:
Kathleen Burke's The White Road to Verdun, dedicated to Madame Jusserand and Monsieur Gaston Liebert, follows a woman's war work in France. Chapters run from true philosophers and the bridge at Meaux to recruiting rat-catchers and a gun carriage turned altar.

Later chapters cover life behind the lines, devotion to animals, hunting for generals, and a meeting with Forain. Verdun itself appears as a white city of desolation, scorched and battered, yet called the brightest jewel in France's crown. Shells, 75 guns, and falling masonry fill its streets, while soldiers hold on with stubborn courage.
12672-a-spinner-in-the-sun:
Myrtle Reed's 1906 novel, A Spinner in the Sun, opens with a little house waiting, grey and weather-worn, leaning toward a sheltering hillside for support from kindly earth. Contents run from The Fire Was Kind and Miss Mehitabel through pearls, depths of love and Araminta. Pipes o' Pan, honour of the spoken word, Piper Tom and housecleaning follow.

Ralph's first case, a loose link, a grey kitten, a river coming into its own, and triumph follow. Araminta's soul, march of days, loved by a dog, Undine, shadow of cypress, secret of veil, poppies, forgiveness and redeemed close the book. Reed writes a sentimental, domestic romance about women, work and healing. The novel offers a gentle, old-fashioned tale of a house, a spinner and second chances.
12936-young-hunters-of-the-lake-or-out-w:
Captain Ralph Bonehill's Young Hunters of the Lake, volume three of the Boy Hunters series, sends four lively boys to Lake Cameron and Lake Narsac with rod and gun. Swimming, a ghost story, a Fourth of July celebration, a lost rowboat, an enemy camp, a swamp, and a bears' den fill the chapters. An old hermit's tale and a mysterious voice add suspense.

A night swim shows the fun: Snap, scared by a wildcat's eyes boring through him, strikes for shore while the doctor's son fires a shotgun to scare the beast. Snap reaches a sandbar panting, sure he was never so scared in his life. The book offers wholesome lake adventure with a ghostly thread.
13455-the-rover-boys-in-the-mountains-or:
Arthur M. Winfield, writing as Edward Stratemeyer, sends the Rover Boys into the mountains in 1902 for fun and fortune. Dick, Tom, and Sam, already known from school, ocean, jungle, and lakes, camp, hunt, and face danger with their guide John Barrow.

Dick crawls flat along a plank over open water to grasp George Granbury's shoulder and save a drowning boy. A wildcat with an injured front leg creeps toward Dick by firelight until Barrow leaps up, rifle in hand, and shouts for a shot. The book is boys' adventure in the classic pattern: camp dinners, narrow escapes, wild animals, and loyal brothers standing together.
1372-the-adventures-of-captain-bonnevill:
Washington Irving shaped this book from the journals of Captain Benjamin Bonneville, a United States army officer who led fur traders into the Rocky Mountains in the 1830s. Irving tells of river crossings, winter camps, hunts, and meetings with Native peoples across a vast and little-mapped West.

The narrative moves from fort to prairie to mountain pass, with tales of hardship, courage, and the fur trade's rough code. Irving's prose gives the frontier a literary polish without hiding its dangers. It is a classic early account of American exploration beyond the frontier.
14865-gwaith-alun:
Gwaith Alun gathers the Welsh works of John Blackwell, known as Alun, transcribed from the 1909 Ab Owen edition. Born in a cottage near Mold in 1797, Blackwell followed his thrifty, thoughtful mother to chapel and Sunday school, learning verses and hymns by heart.

His father, a quiet, serious miner with some English blood, sympathised with the boy. Apprenticed at eleven to a shoemaker who was also a poet, Blackwell bought books by seventeen and walked to Chester to search the shops. Eisteddfod success followed in 1823 and after. The volume preserves his poems and prose in Welsh, a record of a self-taught bard's life and craft.
15036-narrative-of-the-life-of-moses-gra:
Moses Grandy, who could not read or write under slave law, dictated this narrative of his life in American slavery, printed at Boston in 1844 for the benefit of kin still enslaved. An abolitionist introduction frames his story, and Grandy speaks in his own plain voice through the pages that follow.

He recounts sale, hire, hard labor, and his long struggle to buy freedom for himself and his family. The facts are stark, and the moral case against slavery needs no polish. Like other slave narratives of the period, the book served the abolition cause while preserving one man's memory of bondage and endurance.
15655-four-little-blossoms-and-their-win:
Mabel C. Hawley, author of Four Little Blossoms at Brookside Farm and at Oak Hill School, published this winter story in 1920, from the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York. Chapter one opens as Meg and Bobby Blossom come home from school demanding, where's Mother. Twaddles, their little brother, sits cross-legged on a cushion at the stairs' foot.

Mother and Aunt Polly went uptown, Twaddles reports, and promised to bring something nice. Eighteen chapters follow: the first snow-storm, Bobby rescued, Aunt Dorothy's locket, and the bobsled upset. Meg in trouble, the orange and the black, and a birthday party lead to the pond, a new kind of jam, and working for the fair. Bobby's meanest day, a snow man, twins with a secret, and lost in the storm close in the fair at last. Hawley writes cozy winter fun for the youngest readers.
16945-the-white-road-to-verdun:
Kathleen Burke wrote this 1916 book on the white road to Verdun, issued by Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto. She dedicates it to Dr. C. O. Mailloux, the Franklins, and her mother, whose affection and practical sympathy helped all her work. The title points to the road that fed Verdun's defense in the Great War, a lifeline of men, guns, and supplies.

Burke writes of war work, hospitals, and the road itself, with a woman's eye for detail and for those who served. The book gives a vivid, first-hand view of Verdun's rear lines, not of grand strategy. Readers of Great War memoirs will find a moving, humane account of a famous road and the folk who kept it open.
18999-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
William and Robert Chambers issued this number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal on Saturday, June 5, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. Its leading piece reports a visit to the scene of the Holmfirth flood, which had struck the Yorkshire valley in February of that year. The writer traveled from Manchester in April, while the damage was still fresh.

Sympathy for sufferers mixes with curiosity about physical causes, as the author traces what floodwater did to mills, houses, and ground. The piece shows the journal's blend of news, science, and moral reflection. Readers get a vivid contemporary report of a Victorian disaster, and a sample of how a popular magazine taught its readers to observe the world.
1989-the-foolish-dictionary-an-exhaustin:
Gideon Wurdz's Foolish Dictionary, subtitled an exhausting work of reference, is a comic dictionary that redefines ordinary words with jokes. The author, whose portrait fronts the book, prepared the volume not in serious earnest but as a long jest, and its entries turn definitions inside out.

Readers will find the book a period piece of American humor, in the manner of Ambrose Bierce's Devil's Dictionary but gentler. Its charm lies in its sustained silliness: page after page of words defined as they sound, as they feel, or as they misbehave, with never a straight definition allowed to pass.
20792-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 442, opens with a visit to a famed old house. The writers seek not the Royal Society's relics, but the body that now holds its rooms. Such curious, plain pieces fill this June issue of the weekly.

Chambers's Journal brought cheap, wholesome reading to vast numbers each week. Facts, tales, travel, and verse shared its small pages. The Chambers brothers aimed to lift readers without boring them. This one number shows the mix at work: a walk through London rooms turns into a chat on science, memory, and change.
20793-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Nature never runs out, argues Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 443, but our power to enjoy her can fade. Some natures lack that power from the start, the essay says. Whole ages, too, may hold it only in part.

Weekly numbers like this one mixed essays, tales, facts, and verse for family reading. The Chambers firm sold sound reading at a price working folk could pay. Each issue is a small window on what held British minds that week. Number 443's turn toward nature and taste shows the journal's calm, thoughtful tone at its best.
21971-a-son-of-the-sun:
South Seas trading and trickery fill Jack London's A Son of the Sun, a set of tales published in 1912. The title story opens on the schooner Willi-Waw, anchored in a glassy passage between reefs. Her rusty chain wanders over living coral like a monstrous snake while rock-cod play below. On deck, islanders scrape the teak rail under the eye of David Grief, the sun-tanned trader hero of the tales.

Other stories bring the devils of Fuatino, the jokers of New Gibbon, and a little account settled with Swithin Hall. London knew these waters from his own cruising. Grief is his ideal of the white trader: fair, hard, and smarter than the beachcombers and rogues around him. The tales smell of copra, coral, and salt.
23220-the-gray-nun:
Nataly von Eschstruth's The Gray Nun is a tale of mystery built around a veiled figure. White linen bands wrap the woman's head and chin, hiding even her mouth. A black velvet mask covers her brow and upper face, and loose sleeves hide her hands.

What cannot be hidden is her gaze. The blackness of her eyes is so intense that scarcely any whites can be seen. Eschstruth gives readers a figure defined by coverings, where one penetrating stare does all the work. The scene promises secrets, disguises, and a truth kept carefully out of sight.
23262-chasing-the-sun: Chasing the Sun tells of a hero credited with more hand-to-hand fights than the heroes of Greece or Rome ever faced. As a grown man he repeatedly risked his own life to save others, often in plain view of those who had doubted him. Strangest of all, many of his boyhood enemies ended, in time, as his closest friends and allies.
2328-the-lake-gun:
James Fenimore Cooper's short tale The Lake Gun tells of a mysterious cannon-like boom that rolls across Lake Seneca, startling settlers and puzzling naturalists. The story mixes frontier legend with Cooper's love of the New York lakes, as characters debate whether the sound comes from nature, spirits, or human trickery. The lake itself is the hero.

Brief and atmospheric, the tale shows Cooper in his storyteller's mode rather than his epic one. Its explanation, when it comes, is satisfyingly grounded. Readers will enjoy a compact piece of American lake lore.
24150-disturbing-sun:
Philip Latham wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in May 1959, with pictures by Freas. It takes the form of an interview with Dr. I. M. Niemand, director of the Psychophysical Institute of Solar and Terrestrial Relations at Camarillo, California. In December 1957, Niemand read a paper on the nature of the solar S-regions to the American Association for the Advancement of Science in New York.

Latham opens by warning that the piece is fiction, nothing but fiction, and obviously impossible. Niemand then explains sunspots as cooler, darker regions of the sun, rising and falling in a cycle of about eleven years. The tale links solar stirrings to stirrings on Earth. Readers get a sly, talk-driven story of science that may be stranger than it looks.
24892-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, number 441, dated Saturday, June 12, 1852, and priced at a penny halfpenny, shows a Victorian weekly at work. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal, mixing tales, essays, and useful knowledge for a wide readership.

The lead piece, Unfashionable Clubs, praises the shopkeeper's Christmas savings club. Workers bank sixpence a week for a plum pudding and a goose, learning thrift with a spare shilling to show for it. Later pages turn to Scottish character and the literary veteran Jerdan. The issue gives a lively snapshot of mid-century popular print.
26966-a-place-in-the-sun:
C. H. Thames's Johnny Mayhem adventure, from Amazing Stories of October 1956, gives its hero of many bodies a task the cover calls downright impossible: saving the Glory of the Galaxy. The story opens with an SOS crackling through subspace from a point between Mercury's orbit and the sun's corona.

A Fomalhautian freighter picks up the call first, and Mayhem must cross space itself to answer it. Fast, pulpy, and full of starships and strange crews, the tale shows 1950s science fiction at its most breathless, with a hero who can wear a new body for each new danger.
29132-the-gun:
Philip K. Dick wrote this short science fiction story about a crew that finds a dead world and a gun that still lives. The captain peers through a telescope at an atomic fission. The archaeologist Tance leaps back at the sight: a vast expanse of gray slag, pitted and fused, broken only by hills of rock. Nothing moves or stirs, and everything is silent and dead.

The biologist jokes he will find no legumes there, while the captain warns the air is poisoned, as they expected. The story's note promises that only the gun still showed life, and that trespassers wrecked that for all time. Readers get an early Dick tale of ruin, treasure, and a weapon that outlives its makers, told in a few tense pages.
30314-vige-e-le-brun:
Haldane Macfall presents Vigée Le Brun, 1755 to 1842, in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by T. Leman Hare, with eight reproductions in colour. Jack of London and Stokes of New York published the volume in 1907. Its chapters run from beginnings and a wonderful child through marriage and motherhood to Marie Antoinette, sweet exile, and the end. A first portrait of Marie Antoinette at Versailles fronts the book.

Painted in the artist's twenty-fourth year, in 1779, that portrait shows gaiety, roses, sunshine, and the glamour of a throne. No hint appears of the tragedy to overwhelm the young daughter of Austria. Macfall also notes signs of an imperious temper, joined to levity and frivolity of manners that early made her unpopular. Other plates show Madame Vigée Le Brun and child in the Louvre and a portrait in the National Gallery, London.
3046-the-land-of-the-changing-sun:
Will Harben wrote The Land of the Changing Sun as a lost-world adventure beginning in a balloon. Two young men lie insensible in the car as it sinks toward an ocean of white clouds. Harry Johnston, an American dark and sallow as a Spaniard, and Charles Thorndyke, an English gentleman with yellow hair and blue eyes, travel together. Johnston wakes first, opening his eyes dreamily on the cloud sea.

The balloon lands them in a hidden land of strange suns, chasms, and ledges, where a stone dropped from a ledge bounds down until its sound is lost in internal roaring. The companions cross a narrow chasm by a ledge, holding rock with one hand and each other with the other. The novel mixes balloon adventure with subterranean wonder, in the manner of late Victorian romance.
3153-the-virgin-of-the-sun:
H Rider Haggard published this romance in 1922, looking back to the Incas of Peru. A dedication recalls talks some five-and-thirty years earlier about the vanished empires of Central America, and offers a tale of one of them. The legend at its heart runs back before the Spanish conquerors entered on their mission of robbery and ruin.

The Virgin of the Sun belongs to Haggard's late romances of lost worlds and old faiths. Peru's temples, priests, and kings supply the color, while a love story carries the plot through peril. Readers who enjoy Haggard's adventure mode will find it here undimmed: history as romance, and romance with a scholar's taste for vanished splendor.
31973-the-rhode-island-artillery-at-the-:
J. Albert Monroe's 1878 paper The Rhode Island Artillery at the First Battle of Bull Run is number two in the Personal Narratives of the Battles of the Rebellion. Those narratives were read before the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society. It is a veteran's own account. Monroe, late lieutenant-colonel of the First Rhode Island Light Artillery, opens with Lincoln's first call for troops for three months in 1861.

The Marine Artillery of Providence responded cheerfully and, under Captain Charles H. Tompkins, left Providence on April 18 for the seat of war. Readers get a concise, firsthand narrative of the first great battle of the Civil War, told by an artillery officer who was there.
33255-within-prison-walls-being-a-narrat:
Thomas Mott Osborne's narrative tells of a week he spent in voluntary confinement in the State Prison at Auburn, New York, under the prison number 33,333X. First copyrighted in 1914, the book follows his days from Sunday's journal through Monday morning and night, tracing meals, work, cells, and the talk of men in gray. Osborne went in to learn prison life from inside, not from reports or tours.

The account is direct and humane, praising the courtesy and sympathy he met among fellow prisoners. Its aim is reform: to show what a week behind walls does to a man and what prisons might do better. For readers of penal history, it remains a vivid, first-hand plea for a more human system, written by a man who chose to share the cell.
33718-reminiscences-of-service-with-the-:
Pardon E. Tillinghast, late quartermaster sergeant of the Twelfth Rhode Island Volunteers, recalls his service and memorializes Colonel George H. Browne in this 1885 paper. It was read before the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society and printed in an edition limited to two hundred and fifty copies. The narrative opens in the stirring months of July through October 1862, when the Union army's long-promised advance on Richmond was still deferred.

Tillinghast recounts Malvern Hill, where a costly Union victory was followed by the stereotyped order to fall back. That order presented a victorious army running from a defeated enemy. Tillinghast also recounts Pope's disastrous campaign in Northern Virginia. His reminiscences give a Rhode Island soldier's view of command confusion and camp life. Civil War readers will value a concise, first-person regimental memoir with a memorial to its colonel.
34720-we-were-there-at-the-oklahoma-land:
We Were There at the Oklahoma Land Run, by Jim Kjelgaard, was held under a 1957 copyright and printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Chris A Kenyon Jr drew the plates, and Savoie Lottinville checked the facts. The book stands in the We Were There line for young readers.

Thousands of land hungry folk lined the Oklahoma border in April 1889, keen for the signal shot. Young Alec Simpson rides in with his twin sisters, Cindy and Mindy, and their father Jed. The family came up the Cherokee Trail from Missouri for a chance at a homestead. At the shot, riders, walkers, and wagons race to stake claims. Young readers get a true event told as a fast family tale.
35042-winter-fun:
William O Stoddard wrote a boys' tale of winter sports and farm life. Charles Scribner's Sons issued Winter Fun in New York in 1885. Stoddard had written Dab Kinzer, The Quartet, and Saltillo Boys. Nineteen chapters run from a fireplace circle to a flood at the end.

A red cutter, earned by a month of hard work, opens the tale with pride. Mrs Stebbins eyes her son's prize with sharp, fond doubt at the gate. Rabbit hunts, coasting, ice sports, a snow fort, and a sugar bush follow. Boys of the time got a warm, full picture of cold-season fun.
35697-historical-sketch-of-the-fifteenth:
Historical Sketch of the Fifteenth Regiment, New Jersey Volunteers is a regimental history of a Civil War unit. Sharp, a printer and stereotyper of Trenton, New Jersey, printed the sketch in 1880. The regiment served in the First Brigade, First Division, Sixth Corps of the Union army.

Every regiment of soldiers, the sketch begins, has a character of its own, the sum of its men's characters and of its handling. The Fifteenth was organized at Flemington, in the hill country of the state. Three of its companies came from Sussex, two each from Warren, Hunterdon and Morris, and one from Somerset. There were no large cities in the district. Its men, the sketch boasts, were of a high tone of moral character, with the sturdy, tenacious patriotism that belongs to a fixed population tied to the soil.
36754-knut-hamsun:
Hanna Astrup Larsen wrote a life of Knut Hamsun printed at New York in 1922. Larsen edited the American Scandinavian Review and thanks the American Scandinavian Foundation for the fellowship that let her study Hamsun's works in Norway during the winter of 1920 and 1921. Knopf, his sole authorized American publisher, lists Hunger, Growth of the Soil, Shallow Soil, Dreamers, Pan, and Wanderers as ready.

Children of the Time, Victoria, Segelfoss, Benoni, and Rosa were set for later issue. The wanderer, early life in Norway, opens her study. Hamsun has become identified in our minds with the lonely figure that recurs again and again in his earlier books, she writes. The wanderer is forever outside of organized society and forever pays the penalty. American readers get the Norwegian master's life from a countrywoman's close study.
39572-west-of-the-sun:
West of the Sun is a science fiction novel by Edgar Pangborn, set on a far planet. Its action is dated on earth to the year twenty fifty six. The red green world there keeps its own count, called the Year One. The novel is told in three parts that span the first decade there.

Six humans are named on the opening pages as the whole human cast. Christopher Wright is an anthropologist who trusts in man's basic goodness. Paul Mason and his wife Dorothy face hard questions about love and duty. Sears Oliphant is a gentle scientist loved by an alien being. Ann Bryan, the youngest, must learn violence and passion in that strange world. Edmund Spearman is a rebel who wants a tribe of his own to rule. War with his earth companions hangs over that ambition from the start.
41327-new-subspecies-of-the-rodent-baiom:
New Subspecies of the Rodent Baiomys is a mammal paper by Robert Packard. The University of Kansas Publications issued it in December nineteen fifty eight. It runs in volume nine, number fifteen, pages three ninety seven to four o four. The southern pygmy mouse, Baiomys musculus, is the species under study here.

The mouse ranges from Jalisco and Michoacan in Mexico south to Nicaragua. Two subspecies were known from the south: a blackish and a grey brown form. New specimens from Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua reveal two more races. Loans came from the United States National Museum and the American Museum. Kansas Museum holds the rest of the material used in the study.
42159-the-nursery-october-1881-vol-xxx-a:
The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers, is dated October 1881. Volume thirty, number four, came from Boston that autumn. The Nursery Publishing Company at Bromfield Street issued it. Contents split into prose and verse for small children. Edith and the Chickens leads the prose list in the number.

An old sparrow helps a young one in its prose. Home sweet home, the little sailor, and so tired stand there. A found doll and a knowing dog take their turns. Popping Corn leads the verse with a bright kitchen scene. Pour the nice corn into the popper over the coal, it sings. Shake for your life, and listen to the strife. The Crickets' Sociable and a way to Slumberland stand in verse. Roly-Poly comes with music to sing. Edith, aged four, had just come to a farm.
42658-fletcher-of-saltoun:
Fletcher of Saltoun is a life in the Famous Scots Series by Omond. Scribner of New York issued the series volume for American readers. George Omond traces Fletcher from birth and schooling through travels abroad. Fletcher sat in the Scottish Parliament and went to the Continent young.

Chapter two treats the Whig plot and the Monmouth landing in England. Fletcher shot Dare, was found guilty of high treason, and lost Saltoun estate. Adventures in Spain and service in Hungary against the Turks follow next. The Revolution brought him home, and Saltoun was restored to him there. Darien, militia writings, and the Union debates fill the later chapters.
4378-in-homespun:
E. Nesbit wrote these tales in the dialect of south Kent and Sussex, where villages end in den and hurst. She warns that the dialect lacks uniformity, even in misplaced aspirates, but she defends its plain speech against northern consonants and western vowels. Her people are plain folk who talk plainly.

Through summer nights, carts go to market along the road to London. The same road takes village youths seeking work in the city, and girls looking for a place in service. Nesbit's stories follow them between village and city, with humor and sympathy. The collection shows Nesbit before her children's books, writing country life in its own voice.
44764-california-the-land-of-the-sun:
California: The Land of the Sun is a painted tour of the state in colour. Sutton Palmer made the pictures, and Mary Austin wrote the text to them. Black issued the book in London in the autumn of 1914.

Austin had written The Land of Little Rain and A Woman of Genius before it. Eight chapters carry the tour from the sparrow hawk's own country to the high Sierras. Mothering mountains, coasts of adventure, and the port of Monterey come early. Old Spanish gardens, the land of the little duck, and the twin valleys fill the middle. A frontispiece shows the Three Brothers in Yosemite Valley. Plates give San Diego across its bay, a eucalyptus grove, and Glendale. Cypress Point near Carmel and the Santa Barbara mission cemetery close the set.
48303-the-campaign-of-the-forty-fifth-re:
The Campaign of the Forty-Fifth Regiment is a regimental history printed at Boston in 1882. The Company A Associates of the regiment published it. The Forty Fifth Massachusetts was called the Cadet Regiment. Its men served in North Carolina in 1862 and 1863. The preface tells how the book grew out of reunions. Company A men formed a permanent association after coming home.

Their yearly meetings fall on the anniversary of the Trenton expedition. Colonel Kinsley, an honorary member, enlivens them with reminiscence and song. He knew the inner history of the dark days of the war. Talk of printing the regiment's story recurred at those meetings. The regimental association took the matter up as well. The result is a campaign record written by the men who marched it. Camp Meigs at Readville fronts the volume as a picture.
49513-the-complete-herbal-to-which-is-no:
The Complete Herbal is the famous plant medicine book of Nicholas Culpeper, in an enlarged form. Kelly published this edition at London in 1850. Upwards of one hundred added herbs join Culpeper's original stock. Plates show British herbs and plants in colour, with a portrait of the author.

Culpeper wrote for plain families who could not pay learned doctors. Each plant entry gives the herb's looks, its place, and its uses. Rules for making medicines by the true system of nature follow the herbs. Fifty choice receipts from the author's legacy to his wife close the book. A list of diseases with their cures makes the volume a home dispensary. The herbal stayed in print for two centuries as the poor man's doctor.
50401-the-choice-humorous-works-ludicrou:
The Choice Humorous Works of Theodore Hook gathers the comic writings of the English wit, in an 1883 edition. The full title promises ludicrous adventures, bons mots, puns and hoaxes. The memoir that opens the book describes a life chequered by remarkable incidents and passed largely in the broad eye of the world and of society.

The contents show the range of Hook's humour. A section of political songs and squibs follows the Ramsbottom Papers. Hook was famous for hoaxes, and the volume preserves the periodical comedy on which his reputation rested.
50519-the-sword-and-gun:
The Sword and Gun is a history of the Thirty Seventh Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, by Major Eden. Atwood and Rublee printed it at Madison in eighteen sixty five. Eden dedicates it to the regiment's men and to those who fell at Petersburg. Three chapters of history, then rolls and lists, make up the small volume.

The preface calls the regiment's career brief but glorious in the late war. Called out late, it served hard in the closing scenes of the rebellion. Eden built the tale from memory, regimental records, and brother officers' recall. In spring eighteen sixty four the president called for five hundred thousand fresh troops. Governor Lewis ordered the new regiment raised under Colonel Sam Harriman. Tables of gain and loss and a final roster close the record.
53988-the-bride-of-the-sun:
Gaston Leroux wrote The Bride of the Sun, issued by McBride, Nast and Company in nineteen fifteen. Book one is The Golden Sun Bracelet. The tale opens as a liner steams into Callao Roads in Peru. Francis Montgomery, a fellow of the Royal Society, guards locked boxes of manuscripts and books. His nephew Dick Montgomery leaves for shore.

Boatmen with badges swarmed the deck, offering to carry off passengers and luggage. Montgomery sat enthroned on his boxes and would not part from his treasures. It would be two hours before the ship reached the Darsena dock, they told him. Dick shrugged and went ashore to the Eldorado of his young ambition, the Peru of Pizarro and the Incas. A young girl face then blotted out those dreams. Adventure readers get Inca gold, science, and love in Leroux swift tale.
54549-betsy-gaskins-dimicrat-wife-of-job:
W I Hood wrote Betsy Gaskins, a tale billed as Uncle Tom’s Cabin brought up to date. The Wabash Publishing House issued the book in Chicago in eighteen hundred ninety seven. C B Falls drew its plates from life, the notes claim. K L Armstrong shaped an added part of fact at the back.

Betsy, a Democrat by her own spelling, weds Jobe, a Republican. Real events of the past few years ground the tale, Hood says. No claim to gift or genius backs the plain account. Read with mind clear of bias is his one request of us. Jobe is your brother and Betsy your sister, he urges. New Philadelphia, Ohio signs the plea in April of that year. Hood aims the tale at a better state of rule for all.
54899-trials-of-war-criminals-before-the:
Trials of War Criminals before the Nuernberg Military Tribunals, volume one, is the official American record of the later Nuremberg trials held under Control Council Law Number 10. The volume covers the trials run from October 1946 to April 1949 and opens with the founding papers: the London Agreement, the tribunal charter, and the orders that set the courts up.

Its main case is the Medical Case, the trial of doctors charged with cruel tests on prisoners. The contents list high altitude, freezing, malaria, poison, and bone graft tests, the Jewish skeleton collection, and the killing of the sick. Few books carry harder evidence of what the Nazi state did.
54905-trials-of-war-criminals-before-the:
Trials of War Criminals before the Nuernberg Military Tribunals, volume two, is an official trial record. The trials ran at Nuremberg from October 1946 to April 1949 under Control Council Law Number Ten. The Government Printing Office sold the buckram volume to the public for two dollars seventy five. This volume carries the Medical Case, the doctors trial of the set.

Contents here cover necessity, medical ethics, and experiments used as substitute for penalties. Usefulness of the experiments and practice in other countries get argued in the record. A ruling on count one of the indictment stands near the end of the part. Lawyers and historians gain primary text on medicine, law, and war crime.
56950-uncle-wiggily-s-squirt-gun-or-jack:
Uncle Wiggily's Squirt Gun is a picture book by Howard Garis, printed at Newark, New Jersey. Lang Campbell drew the pictures. Charles Graham issued it, with three other Wiggily tales inside: the icicle maker, the queer umbrellas, and the lemonade stand. A rhymed bookplate at the front asks the reader to bring the book back when the laughing is done.

A list inside names thirty Wiggily picture books, from the auto sled to the rolling hoop. One day Uncle Wiggily goes out early to see the sun rise. He passes a rocky ledge hung with icicles, turned all the colours of the rainbow by the sun. A little chap beside him claims the making of them. Garis tells the bunny gentleman's adventures for the youngest readers.
57000-the-boy-aeronauts-club-or-flying-f:
Ashton Lamar wrote a boys' air tale of a youth club that flies for fun. The book is book four in the Aeroplane Boys set. Its mates tell of Morey Marshall and Bud Wilson's flights. All craft facts are true, the set's ads vow in full. A hue front plate and cloth dress mark each book at sixty cents.

In the Clouds for Uncle Sam leads that young set's roll. The Stolen Aeroplane and the Aeroplane Express stand in it. This club book takes the boys off work for pure sky play. A Cruise in the Sky hunts a great pink pearl in tale five. Battling the Big Horn fights the Rockies in cold tale six. Boys of the first air age read them.
57751-queer-luck-poker-stories-from-the-:
David A Curtis gathered poker stories from the New York Sun into a volume published by Brentano's in 1899, with copyrights from 1896 to 1898. Why He Quit the Game opens the contents. Freeze Out for a Life and A Gambler's Pistol Play follow. Queer Runs of Luck gives the book its title theme. Storms's Straight Flush and For a Senate Seat continue.

The Bill Went Through and Poker for High Stakes raise the wagers. Overland Jack and His Last Sunday Game close the visible list. Newspaper poker tales taught the game to a nation of players. Curtis writes of bluff, luck, and the men who lived by the cards.
58066-the-silversmith-in-eighteenth-cent:
The Silversmith in Eighteenth-Century Williamsburg is a craft history published by Colonial Williamsburg in 1980. It belongs to the Williamsburg Craft Series. Its subtitle calls it an account of the silversmith's life, times, and craft. The text opens with two leading craftsmen of the town. James Craig and James Geddy the younger were probably foremost there. They worked in jewellery, watch repairing, and silversmithing before the Revolution. Geddy's shop stood on Duke of Gloucester Street below the church. Craig's Golden Ball stood still farther down the street.

Advertisements from the Virginia Gazette are quoted for both men. Craig imported a choice assortment of jewellery, plate, and cutlery from London. Geddy listed a neat assortment of plate, watches, and jewellery. He hoped the reasonableness of his goods would excuse his shop's place. The booklet reconstructs a trade from ads and records.
58420-the-mystery-boys-and-the-secret-of:
Mystery Boys and the Secret of the Golden Sun is a boys adventure novel by Van Powell. World Syndicate of Cleveland and New York copyrighted the book in 1931. Contents open with the man who could smell money and the boys getting news. Henry Morgan story and Tom breaking the trail lead toward the tropic hunt.

Storm and stress, stranding, and turtles and trouble fill the middle chapter heads. Magic and madness, a false message, and Toosa vengeance raise the stakes in the tale. The Porto Bello puzzle points the hunt at old Panama gold country in the plot. Series boys of 1931 gained treasure, jungle, and mystery in one volume.
58850-a-legacy-of-fun:
Abraham Lincoln's jokes and tales fill a small book with a sketch of his life. Frederick Farrah issued A Legacy of Fun in London in 1865. Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in Hardin County, Kentucky, the memoir opens. His grandfather was slain by Indians in 1784, it notes.

Young Lincoln worked as a bargeman to New Orleans and split rails in Illinois. His comrades chose him captain in the Black Hawk War of 1832. He read law by borrowed books at New Salem as postmaster there. Readers gain the famed humor of a martyred president with his rise in brief.
59519-hunting-the-hun:
Hunting the Hun is a soldier's manual and memoir of the First World War by Captain Belton and Lieutenant Odell, both late of the Canadian forces, published by Appleton in 1918. The chapters explain how an attack is prepared and made, trench routine, life behind the lines, the training camp called the Bull Ring, and the work of the Red Cross.

The first chapter corrects the picture-book idea of battle. Attacks, Belton writes, are not made doubling over no man's land with fixed bayonets and cheers; the bayonet waits for close quarters, and a man with cartridges left uses his rifle. Success needs days of artillery cutting the wire, engineers building roads for the guns, and every man knowing his exact part. Later chapters give trench songs and tips for recruits. The book is a veteran's briefing for the next draft, practical from first page to last.
6069-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-ozarks-o:
Frank Gee Patchin opens in an Ozark camp wrapped in darkness, where Professor Zepplin wakes suddenly and calls for the boys without answer. He warns the young men to be quiet, sure he heard someone moving about, and climbs from his cot to check the tents of Tad Butler and Walter Perkins.

The campfire has long died out, and only soft foliage murmurs in a southwest breeze. Zepplin suspects pranks or bad dreams, and creeps to make sure. The secret of Ruby Mountain waits beyond the night sounds. Patchin builds a boys' mystery from a midnight stir, a watchful professor, and hills full of hiding places.
61685-home-fun:
Home Fun is a book of parlour amusements by Bullivant for families. Dodge Publishing of New York issued it with rights in 1910. A plate captioned Am I Right fronts the tricks and games. A prefatory note states the book's aim in plain terms at once. It means not to produce workers of wonders or marvel men.

No host of professional entertainers shall flood the market from it. It serves those who find real pleasure in amusing others at home. Such knowledge turns lagging winter hours into periods of sheer delight. Card tricks, riddles, and parlour games fill its ordered pages. Hosts of 1910 kept it by the fireside for dull evenings.
63520-an-american-crusader-at-verdun:
An American Crusader at Verdun is a war tale by Rice, a driver of a sick cart at the front in France. He put it out him self at a great school town in the fall of the last year of the war. Its rights were held that year, and it was printed in America.

A print at its front shows its hand in his kit. Its parts run like a log of the road to the great fight. The sea trip, the reach of the far shore at last, and life in a wine land come first. His proof as a driver, his car by its count name, and his rise to a name of the tale fill the next run. A pals last ride and the feast day of France lead to the town of the fight.
63554-going-to-the-sun:
Going-to-the-Sun is a book of poems by Vachel Lindsay. Lindsay also wrote General William Booth Enters Heaven and The Congo. The book came out in 1923.

The title poem takes its name from a great peak and its road. Early pieces tell of a trip to the waterfalls at dawn. A mystic rooster greets the Montana sunrise in one poem. Johnny Appleseed walks west through two linked pieces. Other poems launch rockets that reach Saturn and grow balloons on trees. The verse is wild, bright and full of play. Lindsay sings America with a child's joy and a showman's flair. A preface and short notes frame the singing, roaming verse.
63758-the-moon-and-the-sun:
The Moon and the Sun is a science fiction story by James McKimmey the younger. It appeared in Planet Stories in March 1954. The tale opens at a rocket field in the desert. A gleaming yellow-finned rocket waits on the pad. Six minutes remain before launch.

In the control tower, Charters counts the seconds aloud. His assistant Lampson watches in silence. Charters calls the shot the greatest victory of the age. Lampson thinks instead of Randall, the pilot. Randall waits inside the rocket to guide it to the Moon. Months ago he feared the rocket would serve war. Now the work itself has caught him in its grip. The two men watch the beautiful thing.
64420-jonah-of-the-jove-run:
Jonah of the Jove Run is a science fiction story by Ray Bradbury that appeared in Planet Stories in the spring of nineteen forty-eight. Its hero is Nibley, a very old man hanging around Marsport whom the spacemen despise and ignore.

Nibley has one gift: he can track a meteor across the sky with his mind. He can sense ships and crashes far beyond any instrument, though his talent wrecks the delicate detectors. When the supply ship Terra waits on a repair rocket carrying an asteroid computator, Nibley alone knows it has just crashed on the dead sea bottom, and no one will listen. The story turns on the cost of a true gift in an old, drink-marked man the young men call a jonah.
64889-into-the-sun:
John L Chapman wrote Into the Sun, printed in Comet for May nineteen forty one. Four men are trapped in a space ship falling into the sun. Lejeune, a wiry French biologist, keeps a quart of scotch for the end. Geitz is the ship doctor, Rogers the captain, and Lane the pilot. There is nothing to do but wait, they all know.

There is nothing like having a good quart of scotch with you when you are falling into the sun, Lejeune says. Geitz sputters that Lejeune enjoys being cooked in a cubby holed ship. Not for long, Lejeune answers, for the heat will grow unbearable. Then the ship will be a little spark, he says. Rogers growls that he is a pain. The ship could not hold out much longer against the strain. Fans get a stark tale of men facing a fiery end with wit.
66144-milk-run:
Milk Run is a tale of a drunk space captain by Robert Locke. It first ran in a fiction magazine in May of nineteen fifty three. A log note by the ships mate frames the tale up front in italics. That note says the foe took the ship while its chief lay in a drug sleep.

The Star Rover, a rust freighter, runs from Rigel to the home suns on route. All hands know the chief is drunk, but trust a time wall to sober him. That wall buys a day of grace on each long jump through the void. Two hours in, his clear mind wakes to find the ship lost. Drink, drugs, and a seized ship drive the rough pulp tale.
66450-billy-whiskers-out-for-fun:
Billy Whiskers, Out for Fun is a children's animal tale by Frances Montgomery. Montgomery wrote many Billy Whiskers books for the Saalfield firm. Saalfield of Akron and New York issued this one in 1922. Hawthorne drew the illustrations of the goat's pranks for young readers. A front plate shows Billy upsetting the short, fat cook.

Contents open as Billy, Nannie, Stubby, and Button start a pleasure trip. The chums visit the county fair in the second chapter of fun. What befell them in town and Billy's exciting experiences follow fast. Billy finds Nannie in bad hands, then barnyard excitement breaks loose. A burglar in the cellar, a bridal supper, and an elephant ensue.
67915-sun:
Lawrence wrote this short, strange tale of a sick woman sent to heal in the sun. Archer printed Sun in London in September 1926, in five chapters. Take her away, into the sun, the doctors said, and the tale is off.

She doubts the sun's cure but lets herself be carried over the sea. Her child, a nurse, and her mother go with her. The ship sails at midnight from a black Hudson, its waters spilled with light. Her husband stays two hours, full of dread at the parting. These partings are no good, he keeps saying. She answers in a flat voice. Lawrence turns a health cure into a study of a starved marriage.
69300-korea-and-her-neighbors-a-narrativ:
Korea and Her Neighbors is a travel narrative by Isabella Bird Bishop. Fleming H Revell published it, with copyright in 1897. Sir Walter C Hillier, a former consul general for Korea, wrote the preface.

Bishop traveled through Korea during and after the war between China and Japan. She won the confidence of the King and the late Queen. The book describes Korean character, customs, and institutions. Photographs by the author illustrate the journey. Hillier praises the accuracy of her facts. Few Western writers had seen the country's interior then. Her account remains a key source on Korea at its opening.
6977-flying-for-france-with-the-american:
James McConnell, sergeant pilot in the French Flying Corps, tells of flying for France with the American Escadrille at Verdun. He dedicates the book to Alice Weeks, who lost a splendid son in the French army and gave many Americans in the war a mother's sympathy and help. The contents run from Verdun to the Somme, with personal letters, a chapter on how France trains pilot aviators, and one titled Against Odds.

Illustrations show McConnell himself, Americans flying for France, and two members killed in service, with Whiskey the lion mascot of the squadron. Kiffin Rockwell of Asheville, killed in an air duel over Verdun, appears among them. The book is a young pilot's first hand account of war in the air.
69962-the-virgin-of-the-sun:
The Virgin of the Sun is a play in five acts by Augustus von Kotzebue, set in Peru. Anne Plumptre translated the drama from the German. Phillips published the second edition at London in 1799, priced at half a crown. Plumptre had also Englished Kotzebue's Lover's Vows.

Kotzebue tells in his dedication how the play was born. At Pyrmont one wet evening, a friend watched an opera named Cora with him. She remarked that its story held fine ground for a drama. He caught at the thought and wrote the play at her command. The piece treats the Inca court and its temple virgins of the sun. Plumptre's version fed the English craze for Kotzebue's stage works. The dedication shows the social world in which such plays were made.
70224-the-chariot-of-the-sun:
The Chariot of the Sun is a tale of days to come by Roger Pocock. Its own sub name calls it a fan tasy. Past books by the same hand stand past the title leaf: tales of the west, a book of the rules of the game, and a night of the cold north. It was put out at London in nineteen ten. Its list of parts is a roll of a queen and her realm.

A chief of the realm heads that roll. The lord of a lost land, our dame the queen, and the crown rite come next. The storm that mass es, a room of pain, and the tame of that lost land fill the first run. The moth er of state houses, the crown's own right, and the dawn of the dread stand past them.
71038-additional-mounds-of-duval-and-of-:
Clarence Moore dug and described the old Indian mounds of the Florida east coast for years. This study, first made in 1896, came out again at New York in 1922. It stands in Indian Notes and Monographs, a line on the first peoples of the Americas.

Hodge edited the line for the Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation. Moore's ground here is Duval and Clay counties, and the coast mounds north of the St Johns River. He opened mound after mound and set down what each held. Such dig reports form the base stock of facts on the old peoples of Florida before towns and farms levelled their works.
73683-the-virgin-of-the-sun:
George Griffith, author of The Angel of the Revolution and Valdar the Oft-Born, wrote The Virgin of the Sun as a tale of the conquest of Peru. C Arthur Pearson issued the novel at London in 1898. Its front words are Pizarro's speech to his companions. On one side lie ease, pleasure, and safety in Panama. On the other lie toil, hunger, storm, and a grave in the wilds, but also El-Dorado with gold and glory. For his part, Pizarro says, he goes south.

A prologue, The Line of Fate, opens the tale. The books follow with the doom of the old law, the crowning of Atahuallpa, the choice of Manco, and the Spaniards in the city of the Inca. Later parts give an Inca's ransom, a sentence of death, and cries of sacrifice. Griffith writes romance on a famous page of history.
74000-voyages-to-the-moon-and-the-sun:
Cyrano de Bergerac wrote Voyages to the Moon and the Sun. Richard Aldington turned the French into English. George Routledge and Sons issued it at London. E P Dutton shared the New York issue. Five study parts open the book. The legend and the life of Cyrano lead them.

Cyrano's friends and the libertin question follow. His works close the studies. The Moon voyage prints before the Sun voyage. Extracts from Godwin, D'Urfey, and Swift sit at the back. A bibliography, family tree, and coat of arms end it. Henry Le Bret's 1657 preface anchors the life facts. Le Bret drew his friend in warm colors, Aldington warns. Readers have to look between his lines, he adds. Wild space tales from the 1600s still startle with their jokes at earth's proud men.
74023-a-notched-gun:
A Notched Gun is a western story by Walt Coburn. Coburn swings a dramatic arc from the Old West to France. Sam Graybull was a killer, the tale opens without any softening. He backs out of the Valley Bank with a smoking Colt in hand. A gunnysack full of currency fills his other hand in flight.

The teller made a move for the automatic below the money counter. Graybull's bullet caught that man between the eyes where he stood. The cashier broke for the side door and was shot in the back. The blizzard outside muffled the sound of the shots that day. No one abroad in the storm-swept cow town blocked his departure. He mounted his horse and was lost in the storm in minutes. The Bad Lands country was his childhood's back yard. No fear of pursuit marred the killer's flight from the town.
75492-the-dancing-faun:
The Dancing Faun is a tale by Florence Farr, out in eighteen ninety-four. A front note warns that the tale is all of the mind. It was writ in the summer of the past year, and no man or deed in it is drawn from life, Farr says. The scene is the smart world of London in its day.

The tale opens in a draw room where a young lord and a girl trade sharp talk on truth and sham. He holds that the sole charm of new life is its false face, and she that truth was at all times low. Her mother calls her to sing for a guest. Talk of art as a field where rank counts for naught fills the first scene, in brisk back and forth.
a-spinner-in-the-sun: Myrtle Reed tells a domestic story in this 1906 novel, opening with a little house waiting grey and weather-worn, leaning toward a sheltering hillside. Five-and-twenty winters have broken its spirit, and five-and-twenty springs have not brought back the heart that once went out with dancing feet and singing. Through Miss Mehitable, Araminta, Piper Tom, Undine, and the secret of the veil, the house and its people move toward forgiveness and redemption.
britannica-1911-air-gun:
Air-Gun is defined in its own article within the hosted text, printed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An air-gun propels its bullet by the elasticity of compressed atmospheric air, air squeezed tight and springing back. A reservoir of compressed air is built into the gun or attached to it. Pulling the trigger frees a portion behind the bullet.

That released air expands and drives the bullet from the barrel. Common air-guns, treated as little more than toys, work differently. A spiral spring is compressed, with a piston at one end working in a cylinder. When the trigger frees the spring, it forces air ahead of the piston, and that air shoots the bullet. Some air-guns of this kind are shaped to resemble walking-sticks, in which form they are known as air-canes.
britannica-1911-autun:
Autun is a town of east-central France. It is capital of an arrondissement in Saône-et-Loire. Dijon lies sixty-two miles north-east. The Paris-Lyon railway serves it toward Nevers. Population in 1906 was 11,927. The town sits pleasantly on a hill slope. The Arroux river runs at its foot. Roman remains attest its former greatness. Two stone gateways are well preserved.

Porte d'Arroux and Porte St André are those gates. Each is pierced with four archways. Arcades surmount both gateways handsomely. Ramparts and aqueducts also survive partially. A square tower is called the Temple of Janus. Theatre and amphitheatre remains exist too. St Lazare cathedral crowns the town's highest part. It is mainly twelfth century in fabric. Its Last Judgment tympanum is its artistic glory. Nicolas Rolin added Gothic chapels in the fifteenth century.
britannica-1911-beraun:
Beraun, in Czech Beroun, is a town of Bohemia in Austria, twenty-seven miles south-west of Prague by rail. It stands where the Beraun river meets the Litawa, and counted 9,693 people in 1900, most of them Czech. Textile work, sugar-refining, corn-milling and brewing go on in the town, with lime-kilns, cement works and iron works near by.

Beraun is of immemorial age, first called na Brodě, “by the ford.” The emperor Charles IV gave it city rights in the 1300s and loved the place, calling it “Verona mea,” my Verona, and under him it prospered fast. Later centuries were cruel: Žižka stormed it in 1421, and Imperialists, Saxons, Swedes, French and Bavarians sacked it in turn.
britannica-1911-blow-gun:
Blow-Gun is a weapons article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a simple tube used to shoot small darts. A user blows through the long tube with his mouth. The puff of air sends an arrow or other missile a long way,. Tribes of South America use such guns in war and in the hunt.

They are common among the tribes between the Amazon and Orinoco rivers, and among the Dyaks of Borneo. In the eighteenth century some North American tribes knew them too, above all the Choctaws and Cherokees. A traveller in Louisiana in 1756 praised Choctaw skill with a reed tube some seven feet long. The article says the finest form is the pucuna of the Macusis of Guiana. It is made of two tubes, the inner a light reed that can grow fifteen feet with no joint.
britannica-1911-bohun:
Bohun was a great baronial family of the Welsh Marches in the 1200s and 1300s, and the entry traces its line across two centuries. The name came from a village in the Cotentin, and the family reached England at or soon after the Norman Conquest. Its founder in power was Humphrey III, a steward in Henry I's household who married Milo of Gloucester's daughter.

His grandson Henry won the earldom of Hereford from King John in 1199 and stood among the twenty-five barons who enforced Magna Carta. Later Bohuns held high office and married into the royal house. The line ends with two heiresses whose marriages in the 1370s and 1380s carried the lands toward the houses of Stafford and Lancaster.
britannica-1911-budaun:
Budaun is a town and district of British India. It lies in the Rohilkhand division of the United Provinces. The town stands near the left bank of the river Sot. Its population in 1901 was 39,031. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its history and district. The town holds the ruins of a huge fort. It also holds a handsome mosque, built in 1223. That mosque rose largely from an ancient Hindu temple's stones.

Tradition founds Budaun about the year 905. Its first firm event is capture by Kutb-ud-din in 1196. It then became a strong frontier post of Delhi. Two of its governors later took the imperial throne. The town was burnt in 1571 and declined after Shah Jahan's time. In 1857 its people sided with the mutineers. British rule returned after a victory in April 1858. The district covers 1987 square miles. Over a million people lived there in 1901.
britannica-1911-bull-run:
Bull Run is a small stream in Virginia. It gave its name to two famous Civil War battles. This 1911 Britannica article describes both fights. The first battle was fought on 21 July 1861. Union forces under McDowell met Confederates under Johnston. The Confederates called the battle Manassas. Both armies were newly raised and barely trained.

The article sets out the plans on each side. McDowell meant to feint at the Stone Bridge. Two divisions would turn the position by Sudley Springs. Johnston reached the field by rail on 20 July. His own attack orders miscarried that morning. The Federal attack opened first, and the day unfolded from there. The article then gives the second battle its own account. It treats the stream's crossings as the key to both days. Commanders, ground and timing are set out in order.
britannica-1911-chateaudun:
Châteaudun is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of north central France, in the department of Eure et Loir. It stands on a height near the left bank of the Loire, 28 miles south south west of Chartres by rail. Its population in 1906 was 5805. The streets radiate from a central square in straight, regular lines. That order comes from rebuilding after fires in 1723 and 1870.

The château is the town's most remarkable building. Jean, count of Dunois, and his descendants built most of it. Founded in the tenth century, it joins a great wing with a fine sixteenth century staircase to a chapel wing and a twelfth century keep. The church of La Madeleine dates from the twelfth century. Local industries include flour milling, tanning, and the making of blankets, nails, and machinery. Trade is in cattle, grain, wool, and hemp.
britannica-1911-damaun:
Damaun, or Daman, is a town of Portuguese India at the east side of the entrance to the Gulf of Cambay, capital of the settlement of the same name. The settlement covers 82 square miles and held 41,671 people in 1900. It falls in two parts, Damaun proper and the larger district of Nagar Havili, split by a strip of British land. The soil is fertile, and rice, wheat, and tobacco lead the crops. Its teak forests are valuable.

Weaving has faded, but mats, baskets, deep-sea fishing, and shipbuilding still employ the town. Early in the 1800s a large transit trade in opium ran from Karachi through Damaun to China, until Britain stopped it in 1837. The Portuguese sacked and burnt the town in 1531, then took it for good in 1558. They turned its mosque into a church. Nagar Havili came to them from the Mahrattas in 1780, as payment for piracy losses.
britannica-1911-gabun:
Gabun is a district on the west coast of Africa, one of the colonies forming French Congo, named from the settlements on the Gabun river. That river is really an estuary lying just north of the equator, some ten miles wide at its entrance and keeping a breadth of about seven miles for forty miles inland. The Komo is the chief of the rivers flowing into it.

Portuguese sailors found the estuary late in the 15th century and named it from a fancied likeness to a cabin. Scanty remains of a Portuguese fort have been found on Koniké island, near the middle of the estuary. The chief tribes of the district are the Mpongwe, the Fang and the Bakalai.
britannica-1911-idun: Idun is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Norse goddess of youth and spring. She was the daughter of the dwarf Svald and the wife of Bragi. Her charge was the golden apples, whose eating kept the gods in eternal youth. Loki, the evil spirit, kidnapped her together with the apples, but the gods forced him to set her free. The article reads her as a figure of the year from March to September, her myth standing for the yearly imprisonment of spring by winter.
britannica-1911-jean-de-meun:
Jean de Meun, a French writer who lived from about 1250 to about 1305, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. His first name was Jean Clopinel or Chopinel, and he was born at Meun on the Loire. Custom says he studied at the university of Paris. Like Rutebeuf, he defended one scholar and sharply attacked the begging orders of friars.

Most of his life seems to have been spent in Paris, the entry says. There he owned a house with a tower, court, and garden. In his youth he wrote songs sung in public places and schools across France. Chief among his works, he placed his continuation of the Roman de la rose, a poem begun by Guillaume de Lorris. That second part is dated between 1268 and 1285.
britannica-1911-karun:
The Karun is a weighty river of Persia. Its head waters rise in the mountain cluster known since at least the 14th century as Zardeh Kuh, 13,000 feet high, in the Bakhtiari country about 115 miles west of Isfahan. Until it reaches Shushter it is called the Ab i Kurang, and in an old Pahlavi work it bears the name Kharāē.

From the meeting of its two chief sources at about 8000 feet, the stream runs full, deep, and fast between cliffs of 1000 to 3000 feet. The steepness of its banks makes it of little use for watering fields. Though Shushter lies only about 75 miles away in a straight line, the river winds so much that it travels 250 miles to reach the city. Many side streams, fresh and salt, feed it on the way through the Bakhtiari hills. The entry follows the river from its high springs in close survey detail.
britannica-1911-kazerun:
Kāzerūn is a district and town of the province of Fars in Persia, set between Shiraz and Bushire. In its centre lies the Kāzerūn Valley, a fertile plain 30 miles long and 7 to 8 broad. The Parishān Lake bounds it on the southeast, and the Boshavir River on the northwest, with the ruins of the old city of Shapūr and Sassanian rock carvings on its banks.

The rest of the district is mostly hilly country cut by many streams. Zizyphus, wild almond, and oak cover the plains and hills. The district counts forty six villages and about 15,000 people. It yields rice of fine quality, cotton, tobacco, and opium, but very little corn. Bread made from acorn flour is a staple food in many villages. In a cave by the river stands a statue of Shapur,.
britannica-1911-loudun:
Loudun is a town of western France, chief town of a district in the department of Vienne. It stands on a rise above a fertile plain, forty-five miles by rail south-west of Tours. It had 3,931 people in 1906. Walls once ringed the town, but a single gateway and two towers are left of them. A fine square keep of the twelfth century survives from the old castle.

The castle site is now a public walk, and traces of Roman building have been found at the foot of the keep. The Carmelite convent was the scene of the trial of Urban Grandier. He was burned alive for witchcraft in 1634. The old church of Sainte Croix, where he served, is now used as a market. The church of St Pierre-du-Marche is Gothic in style with a tall stone spire.
britannica-1911-nisbett-louisa-cranstoun:
Louisa Cranstoun Nisbett was an English stage star who lived from eighteen twelve to eighteen fifty-eight. She was the child of an actor who played past a stage name. As that name she won much stage time in the chief parts of Shakespeare. Her first London show came in eighteen twenty-nine.

Her charm and high heart made her a pet of the crowd in gay parts. She wed a sea man and quit, but his death by a fall that same year forced her back. She made a famed part her own in a hit play. Two more bouts of wed life and loss mark her tale.
britannica-1911-sun:
Sun is the name of the central body of the solar system, the orb that gives earth light and heat. A 1911 Britannica entry gives the word in English, German, French, Latin, and Greek forms. Other bodies at the centre of their own systems are called suns by likeness. The entry then faces the hard task of grasping a body no lab can copy.

Its heat would turn all known stuff to vapour, so direct trials are out of reach. Laws of mechanics and physics are the only guides men can trust here. The entry warns that stretching those laws so far may yield dark or clashing claims. The sun body must be uncombined gases, it argues from the evidence.
britannica-1911-tun: Tun is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a town in the province of Khorasan, Persia. It sits south of Nishapur, at an elevation of 1,200 feet. The town has seven thousand people. It is ringed by a wall twenty feet high, raised on a rampart of mud. It has three gates, handsome bazaars, and good caravanserais. Around it lie many gardens and fields producing opium, tobacco, and cotton. Some silk is also grown there.
britannica-1911-verdun:
Verdun, a garrison town of north east France on the Meuse, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a fortress of the first rank. It was the chief town of its district, on the rail line between Paris and Metz, with near thirteen thousand people in 1906, plus eight thousand soldiers.

The town sits in a basin ringed by vine clad hills, and it faced the frontier of German Lorraine and the great camp at Metz. In the war of 1870 it was a small old fortress of Vauban's age, held long with no hope of relief. After that war, a new line of forts was built on the Meuse in 1875, and Verdun became the centre of a fortified camp. Forts were set on all the heights besiegers had used in 1870. The defences were then pushed east to the cliffs above the Woevre plain.
britannica-1911-vingt-et-un:
Vingt-et-un, called Van John in slang, is a card game explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a round game at which any number may play. Five or six players are plenty for a good game. The rules given rest on stakes laid in counters or chips.

The dealer gives one card face down to each player, himself included. The others look at their cards and declare their stakes by their worth. The dealer may then double all the stakes if he chooses. A second card goes round, also face down. The aim is to make twenty-one from the pips on the cards. An ace counts as one or eleven, and court cards as ten each. An ace with a ten card makes a natural at once. That hand is paid double the stake, sometimes treble.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anastasius-gr:
Anastasius Grun was the pen name of Anton Alexander, Count von Auersperg, an Austrian poet born at Laibach in 1806 and dead at Graz in 1876. He trained at the Theresian academy in Vienna and studied philosophy and law at Vienna and Graz. From 1831 he managed his family estates at Thurn, travelling in Italy, France, and England before marrying a countess in 1839.

His poems made him famous as a champion of liberalism, and he entered politics, winning election to the National Assembly at Frankfort in 1848. Disappointed there, he withdrew to private life, then returned as a life member of the Austrian Reichsrat. His early lyrics appeared in 1830, followed by a romantic cycle praising Emperor Maximilian I and, in 1831, anonymous political poems that attacked the rule of his day. His complete works were edited in five volumes in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-wyn:
Andrew of Wyntoun, Scottish chronicler, was born about the middle of the fourteenth century, in David II's reign. He was perhaps related to Alan of Wyntoun, who married Seton's heiress. He became a canon-regular of Saint Andrews priory, and before 1395 prior of Lochleven, its subject house for centuries.

The Saint Andrews register holds his acts as Lochleven prior from 1395 to 1413, but nothing shows when he died. At Sir John de Wemyss's request, he wrote his Orygynale Cronykil of Scotland, so called because it begins at the beginning of things, with the creation of angels. Since Robert, Duke of Albany, appears as dead, it was finished after September 1420. Writing its latter part, he called himself an old man, so he did not live long after. The manuscripts show revision, by his own hand. No printed edition appeared until 1795, when Macpherson edited it, omitting a third, restored by Laing in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attila-the-hu:
Attila, king and general of the Huns until his death in 453, took over disorganized Scythian hordes in 433. He forged them into a feared force across Europe and Asia, invading the Eastern Roman Empire in 441 and then sweeping into Gaul. In 451, allied Romans under Aetius and Visigoths under Theodoric met him on the Plains of Chalons and turned him back.

The next spring he ravaged Aquileia and Lombard cities and marched toward Rome. An embassy near Mantua, led in influence by Pope Leo I, talked him out of sacking the city. For Catholic readers, the entry stresses the bishops of France and Italy who faced him down, above all the pope. It closes with the legends nations later wove around him, best known as Etzel in the Nibelungenlied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-autun:
Autun, ancient Augustodunum, is a diocese covering the Saone-et-Loire department in France. Under the old regime it answered to Lyons. After the Revolution it joined Chalons and Macon, answering to Besancon in 1802 and to Lyons in 1822. Christian teaching reached Autun early, as the Greek inscription of Pectorius from the third century shows, found in 1839 in the cemetery of St Peter. It witnesses to baptism and to the words of the Eucharist.

Legend sends St Irenaeus's priests Benignus, Andochius, and Thyrsus toward Autun in the sixth-century persecution cycle. Tradition names St Amator, about 250, as bishop, while the first bishop known to history is St Reticius, a writer and contemporary of Constantine. The see won the right to the pallium, the archbishop's woolen band, from Gregory the Great in 599. Later bishops loomed in Merovingian politics, and Autun councils legislated against simony, the buying of church office, and monastic encroachments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-de:
Bernardino de Sahagún, a Franciscan missionary and pioneer student of Aztec culture, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Sahagún in Spain in or before 1500, he died at Mexico in 1590 after more than sixty years in the country. Sent out in 1529, he taught at the college of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco.

There he preached, converted, and taught native youth Spanish, Latin, science, music, and religion, while mastering Nahuatl, the Aztec tongue, through daily practice. His great manuscript on Aztec life, finished in 1569 with a grammar and dictionary, went unpublished for fear of reviving pagan memory. It survives as a foundation of Mexican ethnology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lebru:
An entry on Charles Lebrun, the French historical painter who shaped court art under Louis XIV. Born in Paris in 1619 and trained first by his father, then in the studio of Vouet, he caught the eye of Poussin and spent four years in Italy from 1642. Back in France he won commissions from Fouquet and Queen Anne of Austria, and Cardinal Mazarin introduced him to the king, where he soon held sway over nearly all artistic matters.

Lebrun helped found the Academy in 1648. When Colbert set up the Gobelin tapestry works in 1662, he became its director, designing cartoons, the full-scale drawings for tapestries, and decorations for Versailles, Sceaux, and Marly. After Colbert died in 1683 he lost his patron and withdrew from court into melancholy. The entry admires his energy and colour sense while finding his grand manner heavy and not wholly good for French art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gibail-and-ba:
Gibail and Batrun form a Maronite residential see administered by the Maronite patriarch through auxiliary bishops. Gibail is the modern name of Byblos, an old Phoenician city, and the diocese covers the districts of Ehden, Bcharra, Gibail, and Batrun. A Catholic Encyclopedia article counts its faithful, priests, churches, and convents as they stood in the early twentieth century.

The diocese then numbered 70,000 faithful, 470 priests, and 277 churches and chapels, with convents of Baladites, Aleppines, and Isaites. The patriarch lived at Bkerkey, beside the seminary of Saint-Jean-Maron with thirty students, while another seminary at Rumie held thirty-two. Gibail town itself held about a thousand people, nearly all Christians, with thirteen churches, three of them beautiful Crusader buildings. Whether to split the see into Gibail and Batrun dioceses was much discussed in recent years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honorius-of-a:
Honorius of Autun was a theologian, philosopher, and encyclopedic writer of the first half of the twelfth century, and one of the most mysterious figures of the medieval period. Certainty reaches only so far: he flourished between 1106 and 1135, spent most of that time in southern Germany, and wrote a great many works, most surviving.

Most call him an Autun native in Burgundy; in one work he calls himself priest and head of Autun's school. Yet his German references and glosses, plus readings of Augustodunensis as Augst or Augsburg, have led some to call him German. Others place him as a monk at Canterbury's St. Augustine's. Manuscripts variously call him Benedictine and solitary, deepening the puzzle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-clopinel:
Jean de Meun, called Clopinel for his limp, was a French poet born about 1260 at Meung-sur-Loire and dead at Paris between 1305 and 1320. Born to well-off parents and well schooled, he became by 1300 a wealthy, steady, and pious burgess of Paris, esteemed by neighbours and noble friends.

De Meun translated Vegetius on warfare and Boethius on consolation, and wrote a Testament rebuking women and friars. His fame rests on finishing the Romance of the Rose, left half done by Guillaume de Lorris. To 4,669 verses he added over 18,000, turning a love allegory into a storehouse of the age's learning, quoting Plato, Aristotle, Virgil, Ovid, and Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pectorius-of-:
Pectorius of Autun is the name closing the document often called the Inscription of Autun. Nothing is known of Pectorius's history. The inscription, attributed to him, was found on 24 June 1839 in Saint Pierre l'Estrier cemetery at Autun. Written in Greek metre on marble, it survived fragmentary yet complete enough to rebuild the text. The fragments, kept in Autun's museum, rank among the early Church's most epigraphic monuments.

It addresses the divine race of the heavenly fish, urging a pure heart after receiving waters. It bids the friend refresh his soul with wisdom waters and take the Saviour's sweet food with delight, holding the fish. It closes asking that mother slumber, Light of the Dead, and that Ascandios father, sweet mother and brothers in the fish's peace remember Pectorius. Its content falls into three parts: an address to Christians, one to Christ, and an appeal for his dead kin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placidus-brau:
Placidus Braun was a Bavarian Benedictine historian and librarian of the Abbey of Saints Ulrich and Afra at Augsburg. He was born at Peiting in 1756 and entered the abbey as a choirboy at thirteen. He took vows in 1775, was ordained in 1779, and in 1785 became head librarian, cataloguing its treasures.

His published descriptions of the abbey's early printed books and manuscripts, issued between 1788 and 1796, opened the collection to scholars. After the abbey was dissolved in 1806 and turned into a barracks, he kept studying the history of the Augsburg diocese. He wrote a four-volume history of its bishops, a history of his abbey church, and a topographical survey of the diocese before his death in 1829.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-mel:
Robert of Melun was an English philosopher and theologian who became Bishop of Hereford. Born in England about 1100, he took his surname from Melun near Paris, where he taught philosophy and theology after studying under Hugh of St Victor and probably Abelard. Among his pupils were John of Salisbury and Thomas a Becket.

Through Becket's influence he was made Bishop of Hereford in 1163. John of Salisbury's tributes in the Metalogicus suggest he enjoyed great renown as a teacher. On universals, the question agitating the schools, he rejected Roscelin's nominalism and leaned toward moderate realism. His chief work, the Summa Theologiae or Summa Sententiarum, remains in manuscript save portions printed by Du Boulay. He also wrote questions on Paul's epistles, kept in the Bibliotheque Nationale. Scholars judge the Summa valuable for tracing scholastic doctrines. He died at Hereford in 1167.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-of:
John of Sahagún, a hermit born in 1419 at Sahagún in León, died at Salamanca in 1479. He was the eldest of seven children of John Gonzalez de Castrillo and Sancia Martinez. Taught by the Benedictines, he was given the benefice of Dornillos by his father, which troubled his conscience. Bishop Alfonso de Cartagena of Burgos took a liking to the boy. He had him educated at his house, ordained him priest in 1445, and made him a canon.

Out of respect for church law John resigned his preferments, keeping only the chaplaincy of Saint Agatha. Seeking theology, he studied four years at the University of Salamanca and took his degree. He served nine years at Saint Bartholomew's chapel. After an operation for stone, he vowed to become a religious if spared. In 1464 he professed among the Augustinian Hermits, later becoming master of novices and prior in 1471.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-of-au:
Stephen of Autun, bishop and liturgical writer, built Autun cathedral and retired to Cluny. Born at Bangé in Anjou, hence surnamed Blagiacus, he was son of Gaucerannus, lord of Bangé, and uncle of Humbert, archbishop of Lyons. Of his youth nothing is known. He appears in history in 1112 as bishop of Autun, attending a synod at Tournus in 1115.

A letter of 1116 from Paschal II at the Lateran placed Autun under papal protection and confirmed Stephen's privileges. In 1129 he attended the crowning of Philip, eldest son of Louis VI. He built a cathedral, begun in 1120 and consecrated by Innocent II in 1131. Admiring the religious state, he resigned his see in 1136 and entered Cluny, where Peter the Venerable praised his learning and piety. His Tractatus de Sacramento Altaris treats the Eucharist ascetically and liturgically. He died at Cluny in 1139 or early 1140.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-verdun:
Verdun is a French diocese covering the department of the Meuse. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1802 and joined to Nancy, it was restored by a papal bull of 1817 and a royal decree of 1822. Formed from the old diocese of Verdun plus portions of Trier, Châlons, Toul, Metz, and Reims, and made suffragan to Besançon.

Its bishops run from the fifth-century St Polychronius, disciple of St Lupus of Troyes, through saints Possessor, Firminus, Vitonus, Désiré, and Agricus, friend of Gregory of Tours. Later sections cover monastic life, including the Saint-Vanne reforms of the early seventeenth century under Dom Didier de la Cour. The abbeys of Saint-Vanne, whose superb church was destroyed in 1832, and Saint-Paul, founded about 970.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-440-volu:
A dale of mills and mean cottages sets the scene in number 440, dated June 5, 1852. Factory life is degrading a beautiful valley. The visit covers the Holmfirth flood country. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal walks the damaged ground itself, past stone mills and unscavengered streets, rather than reporting the disaster from a distance.

An attorney's reminiscences and a tale called The Incendiary supply the human stories. Memorials of the dodo gather what was known of the dead bird. Monopolies are argued, a Venetian adventure of yesterday retold, and student-life at Cambridge sketched for outsiders. Dreams, and a wind-storm at night in verse, close the number — and with it this run of the weekly, at early summer.
doe-osti-17028722-collaborative-r-d-with:
Craig Perkins of the National Laboratory of the Rockies served as contact for this cooperative final report, CRADA number CRD-13-00507, issued in September 2026. The partner was First Solar, a maker of thin film solar panels.
