Joint work studied what limits performance in devices based on cadmium selenide telluride, shortened to CdSeTe, and related cadmium compounds.

Samples, test structures, and full cells came from First Solar, from the lab, or from layers grown by both sides in turn. Growth, measurement, and computer modeling were combined to probe two suspect areas: doping, the adding of chosen impurities, and the boundary between unlike layers. Findings aim to guide factory changes that raise panel efficiency and cut cost.
doe-osti-2575366-building-collaboration-:
Final technical report DE-SC0023033, by Adeyemi Adebiyi of UC Merced and covering September 2022 to May 2025, is as much about building a research group as about dust. UC Merced, a Hispanic-serving institution, sits beside California's San Joaquin Valley, where dust shapes air quality and regional climate. The project paired the campus with Pacific Northwest, Lawrence Livermore, and Lawrence Berkeley laboratories to gain fluency in the E3SM earth system model and ARM instruments.

The headline science result concerns where the valley's human-made dust comes from. Fallowed agricultural land is the primary source, the team showed, and dust activity rose substantially between 2008 and 2022 in step with drought severity and expanding fallowed acreage. Models such as E3SM likely understate the dust burden because they represent farm land-use change poorly. The project trained a doctoral student and left UC Merced positioned to join the DUSTIEAIM campaign of 2026–2027.
doe-osti-3018051-computationally-designe:
Chris Kloxin of the University of Delaware and Jeffrey Saven of the University of Pennsylvania are the names on this final report for award DE-SC0019355. Darrin Pochan of Delaware served as principal investigator. The team designed peptide building blocks called bundlemers, from scratch, by computer. A bundlemer is a bundle of coiled-coil peptides that behaves like a tiny, programmable particle.

Activities spanned peptide synthesis, covalent crosslinking, noncovalent assembly, and functionalization. Structures were checked with electron microscopy and with x-ray and neutron scattering in solution. Using natural and non-natural amino acids, the team made modular blocks with chosen charges and chemistry. One comparison mixes positively and negatively charged bundlemers of equal charge count, one mixed-charge and one single-charge, to test how charge pattern steers assembly. The goal is a shared toolbox: robust peptide parts from which other researchers can build complex nanomaterials on demand.
doe-osti-3030029-data-enhanced-resilienc:
Fei Ding of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presents slide deck work on community microgrids, prepared for an Energy Department workshop at New York University and Northeastern University. Ding leads the lab Grid Automation and Controls Group. The talk draws on two funded projects, one backed by the Solar Energy Technologies Office and one by the Office of Electricity. Its theme is using data and smart controls so neighborhoods can keep power when the main grid fails.

The plan splits a distribution grid into cells, each packed with solar panels, batteries, vehicles, and flexible building loads. Cells can join into clusters, island on their own, and restore loads in stages after a blackout. Learning-based controls dispatch each cell resources, first to re-energize the network fast, then to stretch local energy for as long as possible.
doe-osti-3365762-evaluation-for-qflex-be:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4428, by John Serafini and dated May 2026, reports test results on photonic chips from AIM Photonics' QFlex platform, then in beta version 0.6. The Computer Science and Engineering Division measured passive and active components, splitting the work into electrical and optical testing. Integrated photonics packs light-handling circuits onto chips for communications and sensing.

The news was mostly failure, reported plainly. Current-voltage tests on doped heaters in phase shifters showed little to no current across more than 100 devices on several chips, where comparable runs draw about 3 milliamps at one volt. Avalanche photodiodes appeared shorted, showing very low resistance, and photodiodes behaved oddly on one terminal. A beta run evaluation that names what does not work is exactly what a foundry needs next.
doe-osti-3366201-micro2macro-origins-of-:
A US CLIVAR workshop report, Micro2Macro, edited from a meeting held October 28 to 30, 2024 at the University of Wyoming, confronts the largest source of climate prediction error: microphysics. Cloud droplets, ice crystals, and aerosols form at scales far smaller than any Earth system model grid box, yet they steer the whole simulation. Daniel McCoy, Robert Wood, Susannah Burrows, and co-authors organize the community's findings.

Sessions asked what is wrong with microphysics in current models, whether the needed processes can even be observed, and how observations are being fed back into models. Later chapters plan future process campaigns and argue for tighter links between field experiments and model development, from probe to planet. The report's recommendations target seasonal-to-decadal forecasts that stakeholders actually use.
doe-osti-3393788-self-leveling-inks-for-:
Dartmouth College's final technical report for award DE-EE0011153 covers self-leveling inks for printing ultra-uniform perovskite solar modules by flexography. William Scheideler, an associate professor, was principal investigator. The project ran from June 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025, funded by the Solar Energy Technologies Office. The report runs 45 pages.

Flexography is a roll printing method borrowed from packaging, fast and cheap at scale. Printing a perovskite solar layer that way only works if the wet ink levels itself into an even film before it dries; streaks and thickness variation become dead spots in the module. The project developed inks with that self-leveling behavior, aiming at uniform modules from a printing press rather than from the slow coating methods of the laboratory.
doe-osti-3684099-dielectric-spectroscopy:
Pacific Northwest report PNNL-39707, dated August 2026, tests a sound-free way to judge ageing in nuclear plant cables. S. W. Glass, M. Elen, and L. S. Fifield are the printed authors. The method is dielectric spectroscopy, which reads how insulation responds to an electric field. The hard case here is uneven ageing, where only part of a cable run has baked in heat.

Cable lengths were heat-aged in set shares, then measured. Aged insulation showed clear shifts in capacitance and permittivity against fresh cable. Permittivity tracked a standard damage measure steadily, where that older measure stays flat, then jumps late. That steady trend suits cables still in place, since the test does no damage. One caution stands out: the reading averages the whole cable. A short, badly aged stretch can hide inside a sound average. Judging failure risk calls for the worst segment, not the mean.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in:
A Phoenix memo dated June 5, 2002, carries this Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Zakaria Mustapha Soubra. The memo went to the counterterrorism staff in Washington. It treats Soubra as a man who moved in the same Phoenix circle as hijackers Hani Hanjour and Nawaf Al Hazmi.

The Phoenix office says, in plain terms, that it did not find Soubra fully frank. Agents doubted his account of his ties to two other men in that circle. They also doubted what he said he knew of an airline incident the memo names. The office held that Hanjour and Al Hazmi had shared Soubra's social world while they lived in the Phoenix area. The file is a field office judgment, not a court finding.

Questions for a man in Prague shape this Federal Bureau of Investigation cable dated June 9, 2004. The PENTTBOM team in New York sent the bureau's Prague office a brief for a talk with a man named Al Salmi, who had known Nawaf Al Hazmi in San Diego.

The brief carries what Al Salmi had said before. He placed Al Hazmi in San Diego from about January 2000, living at first in Los Angeles. He called him a quiet man who kept to his room and spoke little of himself. Khalid Al Mihdhar was, he said, a close friend and at one time a roommate. The two men went out together just twice that he recalled, once for car papers and once for pizza.

Newark sent this Federal Bureau of Investigation summary on May 3, 2002, to pull the PENTTBOM case into one place. The synopsis says the aim was to give summary facts and set leads. Page after page of case serials from offices across the country fills the front of the file.

The serials name work from Minneapolis, Washington, Phoenix, San Diego, and Newark itself. Each stands for a report, an interview, or a records check in the wider probe. The sampled body passes to a Phoenix cable of June 4, 2002, on the same case. The file is less a tale than a map of the case's bulk by the spring of 2002: one crime, worked by dozens of offices, with the paper trail to show it.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th:
June 2001 threat pages from the daily update of the Federal Bureau of Investigation fill this file. The update served the Usama Bin Laden and Radical Fundamentalist unit. Its standing note told readers the text was raw reporting, not a base for action on its own.

The sampled items look abroad. One reports that Bin Laden had been warned he might be forced to leave Afghanistan. A foreign liaison service reported that a Lebanese group, Ashat Al Ansar, planned an attack on an embassy in Beirut, with a truck and explosives in mind. The same pages say men from a second group met Bin Laden's people in a Palestinian refugee camp in Lebanon. There, they talked of how United States interests could be hurt.
flying-for-france-with-the-american-esca:
James R. McConnell's Flying for France tells of the American Escadrille at Verdun, from a sergeant-pilot in the French Flying Corps. McConnell dedicates the book to Mrs. Alice S. Weeks, who lost a son in the French Army and mothered many other Americans in the war.

Chapters cover Verdun, the move to the Somme, McConnell's personal letters, how France trains pilot aviators, and fighting against odds. Photographs show the Americans who flew for France, including Kiffin Rockwell, killed in an air duel over Verdun, and the squadron's lion mascot Whiskey. Readers of First World War aviation will find McConnell's account immediate, modest and moving.
four-little-blossoms-and-their-winter-fu:
Hawley's four Blossom children meet the first snowstorm of winter in this story for young readers. Meg and Bobby come home asking for Mother, while the twins, Twaddles among them, tumble into the fun. Chapters promise a rescued Bobby, an upset bobsled, and children lost in the storm.

Much of the winter turns on a fair. The children choose animal parts for a play, change their minds, and get measured by Aunt Polly for costumes. Three rehearsals a week run until the Saturday set for the fair. Mabel C. Hawley published this Blossom book in 1920, after volumes at Brookside Farm and Oak Hill School.
govdocs-archive_org-UAP_Encounters_Relea:
FBI file 62-HQ-83894 is one of the Bureau's central files on unidentified aerial phenomena, and this release covers serials 246 through 301. The excerpts come from the FBI's Central Records Center and were declassified for the UAP Encounters release.

Inside are the Bureau's working papers on sightings, including photographs and correspondence sent in by the public and other agencies. The documents show how reports were logged, checked, and filed over the years, in agents' own wording. For researchers, the value lies in the raw record: what the FBI actually collected, rather than later summaries of it.
gwaith-alun:
Gwaith Alun is the Welsh collected works of John Blackwell, the poet who wrote under the bardic name Alun. This edition was printed in 1909. Its Welsh preface tells his life. He was born in 1797 in a cottage near Mold, son of a thoughtful miner. His mother, from Llangwm, took him to chapel meetings and Sunday school. At eleven he was apprenticed to a shoemaker who was also a poet. He taught himself as he worked.

By 1823, the preface says, he shone as a poet. Blackwell wrote in the strict meters of Welsh verse, the cynghanedd he loved, and won fame at eisteddfodau while still working at his trade. He later became a clergyman. The volume holds his poems and prose in Welsh. For readers of Welsh, it keeps the work of a self-taught shoemaker who rose to stand among the poets of his nation.
in-homespun:
E. Nesbit published In Homespun in London in 1896, a book of short tales told in village voices. Her preface, written from Kent, explains that the stories use the plain speech of South Kent and Sussex country folk. She warns scholars the dialect is living talk, not a puzzle needing a glossary. Each tale is narrated by an ordinary local person.

Stories include The Bristol Bowl, Barring the Way, A Death-Bed Confession, and Her Marriage Lines. Cousins compete for an aunt's savings, sons go guilty or astray, and lovers find one way of love. Nesbit lets her narrators ramble, digress, and judge their neighbours freely. The homespun manner, meaning rough home-made cloth, gives the book its warmth. Village pride, money, and Providence shape every small drama.
narrative-of-the-life-of-moses-grandy-la:
Moses Grandy tells his life as a slave in the United States here. Oliver Johnson issued the book in Boston in 1844. Sales aided his kin who were still held in slavery. A quote from William Pitt fronts the tale.

Pitt calls slavery incurable injustice that must be wiped out whole. The editor notes Grandy could not read or write. Slave laws had kept him illiterate, so names follow his speech. An abolitionist friend's letter brought Grandy to London in 1842. His plain tale of work, family loss, and bought freedom stands among the key slave narratives of its age.
nasa-tm-19650012051-considerations-for-o:
George Hondros is named as author of this 1965 Goddard study, though the scan renders parts of the cover poorly. His subject was the ground system for receiving television from the Apollo spacecraft. Apollo would be at lunar distance, about a quarter million miles away. A television signal fades badly over that distance.

Hondros considers how to set up the ground system for the best result. Antenna size, receiver design, and signal handling all affect the picture. Getting live television from the Moon was a public goal as well as a technical one. This study works on the ground half of that problem.
nasa-tm-19700026493-experimental-develop:
Bobby F. Walls, William C. Mastin, and Peter H. Broussard Jr. of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on April 30, 1970. It reviews a development program for lunar surface navigation gear. Astronauts driving on the Moon would need to know where they were at all times.

The authors examine several proposed schemes for crewed navigation, with notes on uncrewed needs. They favor schemes that could be built soon from proven hardware. The report outlines Marshall's own work in this field. Its main stress falls on a dead reckoning system using gyroscopes, then being designed, built, and tested in-house.
nasa-tm-19710011473-preliminary-evaluati:
Gordon K Watson of the Lewis Research Center issued this early evaluation in March 1971 as NASA TM X-52998. Two fuel specimens had spent twenty five hundred hours in flowing hot lithium. Each specimen was a uranium mononitride cylinder wrapped in tungsten lined T-111, a tantalum alloy. The lithium loop ran at a heat near nineteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit.

By looks, weight, chemistry, and metal structure, the specimens suited flowing lithium well. One problem did appear. Room temperature strength tests broke the cladding in a brittle way, along grain boundaries. Heating the cladding in vacuum for one hour at a higher heat restored its bendable strength.
the-adventures-of-captain-bonneville-u-s:
Washington Irving shaped The Adventures of Captain Bonneville from the captain's own journal, first printed in 1837. Bonneville was a United States Army officer whose trips to the Rocky Mountains and the Columbia River form the book's core.

Irving says he met Bonneville while at work on his account of Astoria, at the table of John Jacob Astor. Astor, the patriarch of the American fur trade, drew keen travelers to his board, and Bonneville stood out among them. Irving paints him as a soldier with a trapper and hunter grafted on. Readers get mountain men, fur brigades, and Native nations of the far West, in Irving's smooth and fond prose.
the-bride-of-the-sun: Gaston Leroux wrote The Bride of the Sun, dated 1912, in a copy put out in 1915 by McBride, Nast and Company. The list of books gives the shape of the tale in four parts. Book I is The Golden Sun Bracelet, Book II is The Living Past, also with four. Book III, The Trail of the Ponchos, has five. Book IV is named The Dictator,. No chapter heads are given inside the books, and no page of the tale is shown.
the-foolish-dictionary-an-exhausting-wor:
Wallace Goldsmith drew and wrote The Foolish Dictionary, printed at Boston in 1904, a comic work of reference on unsure English words. The title page credits the text to Gideon Wurdz, a mock scholar.

Wurdz bears grand fake titles: Master of Pholly, Doctor of Loquacious Lunacy, Fellow of the Royal Gibe Society. The book vows to give the origin, meaning, and right and wrong use of words, confused by a few pictures. In the line of Ambrose Bierce's sharp word lists, it turns dry definitions into jokes on fools, bores, fads, and the high talk of the day.
the-lake-gun:
James Fenimore Cooper's short story comes here with an editor's apparatus. Hugh C. MacDougall transcribed and annotated it. He founded the James Fenimore Cooper Society. His notes explain the tale's history. It is one of Cooper's very few short stories. He wrote it in the last year of his life. A gift volume called The Parthenon carried it in 1850. Cooper earned a hundred dollars for it. A limited book edition followed in 1932. Robert E. Spiller introduced that edition.

MacDougall warns readers what they hold. The tale rests on Seneca Lake folklore. The Wandering Jew and the mysterious lake gun figure in it. A supposed Seneca legend underlies it. In fact it is political satire, he says. Demagogues in general are its target. Senator William Henry Seward is its target in particular. The story opens with the Seneca's two wonders. A tree floats balanced above the water first.
the-land-of-the-changing-sun:
Will N. Harben opens his strange tale with two young men waking in a sinking balloon above the clouds. Harry Johnston, an American, revives first and splashes water on Charles Thorndyke, an English gentleman. Both are weak, bloodless, and unsure where they are.

They recall a professor who fell from the car while clinging to a rope. Johnston tried to pull him up, yet the tilting basket nearly threw all three men out. Grief and guilt hang over the pair as the balloon sinks toward an unknown land below them, in a place neither man can yet name or describe clearly.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-ozarks-or-the:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in the Ozarks opens in darkness, with a chapter titled A Mysterious Visitor. Professor Zepplin wakes suddenly in his cot and calls out to the boys, but no answer comes. Something has disturbed him, though he cannot say what. The camp lies in stillness, its fire long dead.

The professor steps outside without dressing and listens for several minutes. Then he tiptoes to the tents. Tad Butler and Walter Perkins sleep soundly in one, Ned Rector and Stacy Brown in the other. They breathe the deep sleep that follows a long day riding the rugged Ozark slopes. Zepplin grunts and blames bad dreams and the pie he ate the night before. He troops back to his tent through the chill air.
the-rover-boys-in-the-mountains-or-a-hun: A Hunt for Fun and Fortune subtitles The Rover Boys in the Mountains, dated 1902. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the volume, and its frontispiece is captioned Dinner on the Way. The pages preserved here are title matter only. They include a list of other Rover Boys books by the same author. No introduction or chapter text appears. The mountain hunt itself cannot be described from what is shown. The companion list names volumes on the river, in camp, on land and sea, on the Great Lakes, and out West.
the-virgin-of-the-sun:
H. Rider Haggard first published The Virgin of the Sun in 1922 and dedicates the tale to James Stanley Little. Thirty-five years earlier the two had discussed the vanished empires of Central America. Haggard offers a story of the marvellous Incas of Peru and of a White God who, legend says, rose from the sea there long before Spanish conquerors came robbing and ruining.

An introductory section then turns to collectors of relics washed up by the sea of time. Great collectors, dealers, and museum agents are set aside. The editor-narrator means the small collectors of modest means who love old things for themselves, one of whom supplied the history printed in the book.
the-white-road-to-verdun: Jessie White Mario's White Road to Verdun was published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1916. The title page adds a second imprint line in New York for E. P. Dutton. Only the title page and a contents list are present in this record, so her account does not appear. A dedication to the soldiers of France asks them to stand within the light and come always with their faces toward the sun. Contents head a preface and chapters named Ideas, War Weddings, and Whistling Solder, then an appendix.
young-hunters-of-the-lake-or-out-with-ro:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote this boys' adventure about four lads on a lake outing. His preface says the tale stands alone yet forms volume three of the Boy Hunters series. Those books treat field, forest, river, and lake in winter and summer. The contents promise swimming, a Fourth of July party, and a camp on Lake Cameron. A ghost story threads through several chapter titles.

Later chapters bring a lost boy, an old hermit's tale, and a dangerous deer hunt. Enemies from earlier volumes return to trouble the camp. The secret of a mysterious voice closes the tale. Readers get outdoor action mixed with a light mystery.
